name: Algorithms
description: Asymptotic analysis, searching and sorting, divide and conquer, greedy, dynamic programming, graph algorithms and NP-completeness.

nodes.name: Asymptotic notation
nodes.desc: Big-O, Omega and Theta; comparing growth rates of functions.
nodes.summary: You will be able to describe how an algorithm's cost grows using Big-O, Omega and Theta, and rank common functions by growth rate.
topics: Formal definitions of O, Omega and Theta
Ordering polynomial, logarithmic and exponential growth
Properties like transitivity and sum rule

nodes.name: Analysing loops
nodes.desc: Counting the work of nested loops with summations, including harmonic and logarithmic loops.
nodes.summary: You will be able to count the operations performed by nested and dependent loops and express the total running time asymptotically.
topics: Logarithmic loops that halve or double
Harmonic series and n log n loops

nodes.name: Recurrences & master
nodes.desc: Writing recurrences for recursive algorithms and solving them with the master theorem.
nodes.summary: You will be able to write a recurrence for a recursive algorithm and solve it quickly using the three cases of the master theorem.
topics: The three cases of the master theorem

nodes.name: Substitution & trees
nodes.desc: Recurrences the master theorem does not cover: substitution and recursion-tree methods.
nodes.summary: You will be able to solve recurrences that fall outside the master theorem using substitution, recursion trees and iteration.
topics: Change of variables for root recurrences

nodes.name: Searching
nodes.desc: Linear and binary search, two-pointer scans and lower bounds for searching.
nodes.summary: You will be able to choose and analyse search techniques on arrays, including binary search variants and two-pointer scans.

nodes.name: Sorting
nodes.desc: The comparison sorts, their best, average and worst cases, stability and in-place behaviour.
nodes.summary: You will be able to compare the major comparison sorts by best, average and worst case time, stability and extra space.
topics: Best, average and worst case behaviour
Merge sort versus heap sort trade-offs
Choosing a sort for nearly sorted input

nodes.name: Elementary sorts
nodes.desc: Insertion, bubble and selection sort; inversions and counting swaps.
nodes.summary: You will be able to trace insertion, bubble and selection sort and count their comparisons, swaps and inversions.
topics: Insertion sort and its adaptive behaviour
Selection sort and its minimum swaps
Inversions and their link to insertion sort

nodes.name: Quicksort
nodes.desc: Partitioning, pivot choice, worst-case inputs and the expected O(n log n) of randomised quicksort.
nodes.summary: You will be able to trace quicksort partitioning, identify worst-case inputs and explain why randomised quicksort runs in expected O(n log n).
topics: Pivot choice and its effect on balance
Worst case on sorted or equal inputs
Recurrences for best and worst splits

nodes.name: Sorting lower bounds
nodes.desc: The Ω(n log n) decision-tree bound for comparison sorts, and counting and radix sort that beat it.
nodes.summary: You will be able to prove the Omega(n log n) lower bound for comparison sorting and apply counting and radix sort to beat it.
topics: Deriving the log n! lower bound
Radix sort with a stable inner sort

nodes.name: Hashing
nodes.desc: Hash tables under uniform hashing: expected probes, load factor and collision probabilities.
nodes.summary: You will be able to analyse hash tables under uniform hashing, including expected probe counts, load factor and collision probabilities.
topics: Hash functions and the load factor
Separate chaining and expected chain length
Open addressing with linear and quadratic probing
Expected probes for successful and unsuccessful search

nodes.name: Divide & conquer
nodes.desc: Merge sort, fast exponentiation, min-max with fewer comparisons and other divide-and-conquer designs.
nodes.summary: You will be able to design divide-and-conquer algorithms such as merge sort and fast exponentiation and analyse them with recurrences.
topics: Merge sort and the merge procedure
Simultaneous min and max in 3n/2 comparisons

nodes.name: Selection problems
nodes.desc: Finding the minimum, maximum, k-th smallest and majority element with as few comparisons as possible.
nodes.summary: You will be able to find minimum, maximum, k-th smallest and majority elements using the fewest comparisons possible.
topics: Finding min and max together efficiently
Second smallest via a tournament tree
Quickselect and its expected linear time
Median of medians for worst-case linear selection

nodes.name: Greedy algorithms
nodes.desc: The greedy choice and exchange arguments: activity selection, job sequencing and fractional knapsack.
nodes.summary: You will be able to recognise when a greedy choice is optimal, prove it with an exchange argument and apply it to classic problems.
topics: Greedy choice property and optimal substructure
Activity selection by earliest finish time

nodes.name: Huffman coding
nodes.desc: Huffman codes and optimal merge patterns, built greedily with a priority queue.
nodes.summary: You will be able to build Huffman codes and optimal merge patterns with a priority queue and compute their total cost.
topics: Building a Huffman tree with a min-heap
Average code length and total bits
Optimal merge pattern for sorted files
Why the greedy merge is optimal

nodes.name: Dynamic programming
nodes.desc: Optimal substructure, overlapping subproblems, memoisation and bottom-up tables.
nodes.summary: You will be able to identify problems with optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems and solve them with memoisation or bottom-up tables.
topics: Counting distinct subproblems for running time

nodes.name: Classic DP problems
nodes.desc: LCS, matrix chain multiplication, 0/1 knapsack, subset sum and optimal BSTs.
nodes.summary: You will be able to formulate and fill the tables for LCS, matrix chain multiplication, 0/1 knapsack, subset sum and optimal BSTs.
topics: Subset sum with a boolean table
Edit distance and related string DPs

nodes.name: BFS & DFS
nodes.desc: Breadth-first and depth-first search, their trees and running times, connected components.
nodes.summary: You will be able to run BFS and DFS on adjacency lists and matrices, read their trees and find connected components.
topics: BFS shortest paths in unweighted graphs
O(V + E) versus O(V^2) running time

nodes.name: DFS applications
nodes.desc: Edge classification, topological sort, strongly connected components and articulation points.
nodes.summary: You will be able to use DFS to classify edges, topologically sort a DAG, find strongly connected components and locate articulation points.
topics: Tree, back, forward and cross edges

nodes.name: Shortest paths
nodes.desc: Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford, negative edges and cycles, and shortest paths in DAGs.
nodes.summary: You will be able to compute single-source shortest paths with Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford and handle negative edges and DAGs correctly.
topics: Dijkstra's algorithm with a priority queue
Why Dijkstra fails on negative edges
Shortest paths in DAGs by topological order

nodes.name: All-pairs paths
nodes.desc: Floyd–Warshall and Johnson's reweighting for all-pairs shortest paths.
nodes.summary: You will be able to compute shortest paths between every pair of vertices using Floyd-Warshall and Johnson's reweighting.
topics: Tracing the distance matrix by intermediate vertex
Detecting negative cycles from the diagonal

nodes.name: Minimum spanning trees
nodes.desc: Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms and their running times.
nodes.summary: You will be able to build minimum spanning trees with Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms and state their running times for different data structures.
topics: Prim's algorithm with a priority queue
Running times with heaps and arrays

nodes.name: MST properties
nodes.desc: The cut and cycle properties, uniqueness of MSTs, and counting or bounding MST weights.
nodes.summary: You will be able to apply the cut and cycle properties to reason about MST uniqueness, edge membership and total weight.
topics: Effect of changing edge weights on the MST

nodes.name: P and NP
nodes.desc: Decision problems, polynomial-time verification, the classes P and NP, and pseudo-polynomial algorithms.
nodes.summary: You will be able to explain decision problems, the classes P and NP, polynomial-time verification and why pseudo-polynomial algorithms are not polynomial.
topics: The class NP and polynomial certificates
The open P versus NP question

nodes.name: NP-completeness
nodes.desc: NP-hard and NP-complete problems and what a polynomial algorithm for one would imply.
nodes.summary: You will be able to distinguish NP-hard from NP-complete problems and reason about what a polynomial algorithm for one would imply.
topics: Consequences of a polynomial algorithm for one
Problems in P that look hard

nodes.name: Reductions
nodes.desc: Polynomial-time reductions among SAT, 3-SAT, vertex cover, clique and independent set.
nodes.summary: You will be able to construct and reason about polynomial-time reductions among SAT, 3-SAT, vertex cover, clique and independent set.
topics: Direction of a reduction and what it proves
Clique, independent set and vertex cover links
